summaries.headline: Kyndryl, Skillsoft Launch Free High School AI Training
summaries.summary: Kyndryl and Skillsoft are offering free AI education to eligible U.S. high schools, giving grades 9-12 students and teachers access to AI fundamentals, prompt engineering and practical AI-tool training through Skillsoft's Percipio platform. The program, tied to Kyndryl's commitment to the White House AI education initiative, runs through May 29, 2027, and is capped at 25,000 aggregated student and educator users, with digital credentials available to participants. Company leaders frame the effort as addressing a workforce skills gap that starts well before a student's first job, positioning early AI exposure as groundwork for future study and employment rather than a standalone tech elective.

summaries.headline: $4.5M EdTech Competition Raises the Evidence Bar
summaries.summary: The Learning Engineering Tools Competition has opened its seventh cycle with more than $4.5 million available across four tracks spanning K-12 teaching, assessment, postsecondary pathways and education datasets, with abstracts due October 13. Prizes range from $50,000 Catalyst awards for early-stage tools to $300,000 Transform Prizes for platforms with 10,000 or more users, and applicants must show not just what AI can do but how it can be used responsibly and sustained in real classrooms. Since 2020 the competition has awarded over $24 million to 171 teams whose tools now reach more than 51 million learners and educators, a track record that signals funders are increasingly prioritizing proof of safe, scalable impact over novelty alone.

summaries.headline: Declining Enrollment Forces States to Rethink Funding
summaries.summary: Public school enrollment is falling nationwide as birth rates decline, and because state funding formulas are tied to student counts, districts are facing growing fiscal strain. Communities are increasingly confronting difficult decisions around school closures, educator layoffs, and district consolidations as a result. State lawmakers are now under pressure to adapt funding systems built for growth to a demographic reality defined by decline.

summaries.headline: Play-Based Learning Makes a Classroom Comeback
summaries.summary: After years of declining play time in kindergarten classrooms during the 2000s and 2010s as academic demands intensified, educators are now reviving play-based instruction, with some states passing legislation to mandate or protect it in early grades. At Coltrane-Webb STEM Elementary School in Concord, N.C., teachers embed academic practice directly into play—kindergarten teacher Jennifer Petersen described using 10 pieces of fruit or vegetables during play time so students practice counting without realizing it's instruction. As more states codify protections for play, early-grade teachers are finding that guided play can reinforce both academic content and social skills simultaneously, rather than competing with instructional time.

summaries.headline: Colorado Public Schools Race to Tap Tax-Credit Scholarships
summaries.summary: Public school advocates in Colorado are rushing to set up scholarship-granting organizations under the new federal tax-credit program before the state's December deadline to submit an approved list to Washington, hoping to prove the mechanism benefits traditional public schools before Gov. Jared Polis leaves office. The program, created under last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and set to launch Jan. 1, lets taxpayers claim up to $1,700 in credits for donations that could fund tutoring, AP test fees, or fifth-day programming in the more than 130 Colorado districts running four-day weeks, according to organizers like Antonio Parés, who argues public schools have more potential donors than private schools. Democratic nominee Phil Weiser has already called himself a "firm no" on the program, meaning the current scramble by groups like the Colorado Public Schools Foundation and Denver Public Schools Foundation may be a narrow window to build a track record before a less sympathetic governor decides whether to renew the state's participation in 2028.

summaries.headline: Coventry Updates Data Privacy Policy, Passes Grants Audit
summaries.summary: The Coventry School Committee gave first-reading approval to a revised student data privacy policy that adds language addressing artificial intelligence, with a second vote still required before adoption. A state audit of the district's federal grant programs came back largely positive, with Coventry meeting 10 of 11 applicable Title One indicators and fully satisfying Title Four and McKinney-Vento requirements, though a corrective action plan is now underway to fix schoolwide plans at its three Title One schools. As districts nationally scramble to update data governance for AI tools, Coventry's move to fold AI language into existing privacy policy—rather than draft standalone guidance—offers a lighter-lift model other boards may watch.

summaries.headline: Connecticut Expands Attendance Grant Program to 29 Districts
summaries.summary: Bristol Public Schools will receive $225,000 as part of $6.2 million in state grants distributed to 29 Connecticut districts through the Learner Engagement and Attendance Program, which funds home visitors and family engagement staff to address chronic absenteeism. Since LEAP launched in 2021, chronic absenteeism statewide has dropped four consecutive years, from 23.7% to 16.4%, with the program growing from 15 districts to 29 as the state shifts it from federal COVID relief funding to a sustained budget line-item. Bristol's funds will target Bristol Central High School, Bristol Eastern High School and Chippens Hill Middle School, along with 150 to 200 students identified as highest-risk, reflecting a broader state bet that sustained, relationship-based outreach — not just one-time pandemic recovery spending — is what moves attendance numbers long-term.

summaries.headline: IT Leaders Turn Staff Shortages Into Upskilling Opportunities
summaries.summary: Higher education IT departments facing layoffs, hiring freezes and shrinking budgets are responding by investing in the staff they already have rather than waiting to backfill vacant roles. Leaders are auditing existing team skills, pairing veteran employees who understand legacy systems with less experienced staff for cross-training, and building job shadowing directly into vendor implementation contracts so institutional knowledge transfers in-house instead of leaving with outside consultants. As restructuring becomes unavoidable, redesigning job descriptions and org charts around emerging needs — like data literacy and cloud cost analysis — offers a way to modernize without new hires, a model K-12 tech leaders facing similar budget and staffing pressure may find worth watching.

summaries.headline: School Board Candidate Centers Literacy, Safety, Retention
summaries.summary: Sal Arias, a candidate for Kern High School District's Area 1 board seat, has outlined his campaign priorities ahead of the race. Arias points to improving literacy, addressing substance use and student safety, and supporting school employees as the areas he would focus on if elected. The full details of his platform remain behind a subscriber paywall, leaving open questions about specific policies or proposals he'd pursue on these fronts.

summaries.headline: Stanford Shifts AI Oversight From Data to Action
summaries.summary: Stanford University has built a new security framework that evaluates AI systems not just by what data they can access, but by what actions they can take, including changing records, sending messages and triggering transactions. The AI Security Framework sorts systems into low, moderate and high-risk tiers based on autonomy, tool access and reversibility, placing responsibility on the people deploying AI rather than solely on central security teams, with users completing self-certification checklists for self-service tools. As K-12 districts increasingly adopt AI tools that integrate with student information systems and other records of consequence, Stanford's approach — shared with the Ivy+ CISO network and already being adopted elsewhere — offers a model for governing systems that act, not just ones that answer.

summaries.headline: Murthy to Chair Youth AI Safety Institute
summaries.summary: Common Sense Media has named former US Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy to chair its new Youth AI Safety Institute, which plans to set child-safety standards for AI products, test them against those standards, and publish scorecards for families, educators, and policymakers. The move responds to usage data showing 59% of children and teens use AI to search for information and 55% use it for homework help, while separate research cited by the institute found 42% of students turn to AI for mental health support or companionship. For district leaders fielding questions about AI tools in classrooms, the institute's planned public testing results could offer an independent reference point that currently doesn't exist, though its funders include AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic whose products it may evaluate.

summaries.headline: Google's AI Growth Drives Major Nuclear Power Deal
summaries.summary: Google has signed a 20-year agreement with Constellation Energy to fund upgrades across 11 nuclear reactors in Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey, adding 890 MW of capacity to meet rising electricity demand from its AI and data center operations. The $4.3 billion investment is expected to sustain roughly 4,400 jobs and support about 7,200 construction positions, with Constellation also adopting Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise for plant planning, performance monitoring and infrastructure security. As school systems increasingly rely on cloud-based AI tools, this deal is a reminder that the computing power behind those tools carries real infrastructure and energy costs that tech giants are now moving aggressively to secure.

summaries.headline: Illinois Educators Press for More Evidence-Based Funding
summaries.summary: The Illinois State Board of Education held its first public hearing Monday to gather input for next year's budget recommendations, and evidence-based funding dominated the testimony from teachers, superintendents, and paraprofessionals across the state. Funding requests ranged from roughly $500 million to full funding of all districts, with more than 700 districts now farther from their funding targets than a year ago and Chicago Public Schools' adequacy rate slipping from 73% to just over 70%; speakers also pushed for $20 million more for career and technical education, $67 million for free school meals, and $46 million for afterschool programs. With the state on track to miss its original 2027 goal of fully funding schools, ISBE's January recommendations to the governor and legislature will test how much political will exists to close a gap the state's own formula says it created.

summaries.headline: UNESCO Renews Literacy Push in Cameroon
summaries.summary: The UNESCO Regional Office for Central Africa used Cameroon's national International Literacy Day 2026 celebration to reaffirm its support for functional literacy and non-formal basic education programs. The Yaoundé event, led by Ministry of Basic Education officials, included learning kit distributions and exhibitions showcasing skills gained at literacy centers, against a backdrop of global progress that saw youth literacy rates climb from 75% to 93% and adult literacy from 65% to 88% between 1975 and 2024. UNESCO's continued commitment signals that non-formal education pathways remain a priority lever for reaching learners outside traditional school systems, particularly in regions still working to close literacy gaps.

summaries.headline: Anthropic Trains Enterprise Engineers, Not Classrooms, in AI
summaries.summary: Anthropic is committing $100 million to Claude Frontier Academy, a program designed to train 10,000 "Frontier Deployed Engineers" by the end of 2027 who can move AI projects from idea to production inside large organizations. The first cohorts, already running in San Francisco, New York and London, draw experienced engineers from firms like Accenture, Deloitte, McKinsey and Morgan Stanley through a multi-day simulated deployment followed by a 12-week residency leading a real Claude project, with credentials expected in early 2027. This is a corporate workforce initiative rather than a K-12 program, but district leaders tracking the broader AI talent pipeline — and the skills employers are now formalizing as essential — may find it instructive for where workforce and CTE pathways are heading.

summaries.headline: Pearson Buys Workera to Verify AI Skills
summaries.summary: Pearson has agreed to acquire Workera, an AI-native skills intelligence platform that measures and verifies workforce capabilities through role-specific scenarios and simulations rather than course completion or self-reported skills. Workera, founded in 2019 and based in Palo Alto, serves enterprise and government clients including ServiceNow, Accenture and the United States Space Force, and its co-founder and CEO Kian Katanforoosh will join Pearson's Enterprise Learning & Skills leadership once the deal closes in the second half of 2026. The acquisition signals a broader shift in workforce development toward continuous, demonstrable proof of skill over credentialing alone, a distinction district and higher-ed leaders tracking workforce-readiness pipelines will want to watch.

summaries.headline: OpenAI Foundation Funds 163 Nonprofits' AI Experiments
summaries.summary: The OpenAI Foundation is distributing $50 million to 163 nonprofits across 35 states and Washington, D.C. through its second People-First AI Fund, with grants reaching education-adjacent work in student mental health, libraries and media literacy. Rural Opportunity Institute, one recipient, says its use of AI in back-office operations has helped partner North Carolina schools double Medicaid revenue and triple the number of students receiving mental health services, while the Library Foundation of Los Angeles is using its award to expand free AI access across 73 library locations; the grants are unrestricted and not tied to OpenAI products, letting organizations choose their own tools or skip them entirely. With 1,669 applications for 163 slots, the fund signals where philanthropic dollars are testing AI's role in services that schools and districts increasingly treat as core to student support rather than peripheral.

summaries.headline: OpenAI Publishes 722 AI-Generated Math Papers
summaries.summary: OpenAI has released 722 mathematical manuscripts generated by an internal frontier AI model, organized into 372 groups of related results covering open problems across mathematics and theoretical computer science. The company presented roughly 4,000 problems to the model during testing, included formal Lean proofs for many results, and acknowledged that unformalized manuscripts could still contain errors. An independent advisory group of mathematicians from institutions including Cambridge, Oxford, and Stanford called the release significant but stressed that verification is just beginning, warning that researchers must retain the freedom to pursue their own questions rather than simply interpreting discoveries handed down from AI labs.

summaries.headline: Common Sense Media Flags ChatGPT's Teen Safeguards
summaries.summary: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute has rated ChatGPT an "Unacceptable Risk" for under-18s after testing more than 4,000 prompts around the August 18 launch of ChatGPT for Teens, calling on OpenAI to suspend children's access until independent testing confirms the safeguards work. Testers found that on an unlinked account registered as a 17-year-old, ChatGPT completed 35 of 40 homework assignments using Study mode after launch, compared with zero before, and accounts registered as 19-year-olds who repeatedly stated they were 13 never triggered the teen experience; separately, more than a dozen newly linked accounts discussing suicidal thoughts or self-harm received no parental notifications. The findings land as districts weigh AI tools in classrooms, underscoring that platform-side safety claims may outpace what actually holds up under scrutiny.

summaries.headline: DeepMind Watermarks AI Proteins, Raises K-12 STEM Questions
summaries.summary: Google DeepMind has developed SynthID Bio, a system that embeds detectable watermarks into AI-designed proteins without significantly disrupting their biological function, addressing a growing provenance problem as generative AI creates novel biological sequences that existing biosecurity screening may not catch. In Nature-published lab tests, watermarked protein binders targeting VEGF-A, PD-L1 and the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein showed no significant population-level differences in binding affinity compared to non-watermarked versions, and a structural watermarking approach built on AlphaFold 3 achieved over 99.8% detection accuracy, though researchers acknowledge the watermark can be stripped through resequencing techniques. For K-12 leaders building AI literacy and biotech-adjacent STEM curricula, this research signals how rapidly provenance and authentication challenges are spreading from text and images into scientific domains like synthetic biology, a shift likely to surface in advanced science coursework and academic integrity conversations well before it reaches policy maturity.

DENVER – Ohio earned an A in the [2026 National Report Card on State Efforts to Improve Financial Literacy in High Schools](https://us.cisionone.cision.com/c/eJwsyztuKyEUANDVQMeI_wwFhZvZhnXhXp55no8D2M7yI0dpj3Qw6iVb6TlFNQe5uHl2gd8izkYqhFSCSl7LhASKXAnegyslZ16jh0ROK-k9zOaqbAmqSO3kbEEyK3tFutcvsUPdqHWBmEJAXKzQfdz19HG-xdsYj87MhemV6fX9fk8HFZrO9o_ptR51VBj1RZ3p9YBRzwM20ehxtiEyNGR6RSrw3MYE_fHNd8IKotFG0ElUjL9w_QNmLsaGxQfeImLNd2ZlevZ6UO_i__lsB2xTPnfeRyPaP19ra8MMWSRpirCQnViyU8IlMFkFctIa_or6JwAA__-SemhM), issued by the Denver-based [National Endowment for Financial Education](https://us.cisionone.cision.com/c/eJwsy8FuAiEQANCvgRsbGAZYDhy8-BtmgKFSd7WFtf5-Y9PrS15NsBbUXnIyIerVheCivKZMBnwzpcXqDJPRDUKgaIrHmAlJ9uQpswOjvadgLwZbNE2D0wFJC9SzV771b7VT33hMVWuOsdYVFczjBsvb5Zaux_E1hT0JOAs4v16v5c6Nl8f4EHCWO9dOavDGNFn1mv7g8g_CnizG1Uc5Uq293ATq_Jz9znOqz8dz3GlbymOX8xjM-_sDIMZARWVtm0IqTq3FGeUy2WIiO41W_iT4DQAA__9uVVUf).

NEFE issued this sixth report card, which reflects how well personal finance is taught in high schools. The previous five report cards were issued by the Center for Financial Literacy at Champlain College in Burlington, Vt. The first report was issued in 2013.

“Adopting a stand-alone, full-semester high school personal finance graduation requirement is a vital first step in delivering effective financial education to all students,” said Billy Hensley, president and CEO of NEFE. “NEFE applauds Ohio and supports educational leaders as they work to effectively implement these programs in the classroom.”

John Pelletier, senior fellow at NEFE, said beginning with the Class of 2026, Ohio requires all students to take a half-credit of financial literacy course in order to graduate from high school.

“Ohio’s learning standards for financial literacy were revised in 2025,” Pelletier said. The standards include financial responsibility and decision-making, planning and money management, the informed consumer, investing, credit and debt, risk management and insurance and free market capitalism.”

Pelletier said this curriculum covers most of the personal finance topics in financial literacy national standards and deserves an A grade since all students must complete this substantive stand-alone course.

Pelletier said it’s not clear how Ohio measures student achievement in financial literacy or how the state monitors local school district implementation of the financial literacy education requirement.

Pelletier projects that when the Class of 2031 graduates, 29 states will require high school students to take a stand-alone personal finance course, with an estimated 73% of public high school students who graduate in 2031 taking a substantive personal finance course prior to graduation.

When the first report card was issued in 2013, only three states earned an A grade, representing just 5% of students in the nation’s public schools.

“Financial literacy is linked to positive outcomes like wealth accumulation, stock market participation, effective retirement planning and avoiding high-cost alternative financial services. Conversely, poor financial literacy and negative financial behaviors often go hand in hand,” Pelletier said. “High school personal finance education can help alleviate the cycle of poverty that exists in our nation. Requiring all students to take a stand-alone financial literacy course, regardless of their race, ethnicity or economic status, is an important step our nation can take toward reducing inequality.”

A [2025 nationwide opinion poll](https://us.cisionone.cision.com/c/eJwsy0GynCAQANDT4K4tbEBl4eJvvMavFpqRGYSJYExun5rU376q5xecnZZjx8swWTmbaTK22xflt4BqpmnkQBgmJXFjyco4bWgYTBeXkTY2OMhxpEl9DzrYIUg0ctIkhZY1en7FX3BQTHxW8H6z1vtZA9b2wv7jXVr21t5VqC-Bq8D1vu8-c-C-nA-Ba-a7ClxRohG4Si1wfZeU4KBnOWP7CyXAVYH8lVqFm3KDEDNlFykB-8tRiyVDzLDHxw7V7aWk2lN9_-kO9pHg5MRUGaJf_sP3Dwj1pbSdR9udi_fRvYSW21Vj5lrhWa4zU-pdObraTubj8xG1thM52KQKoMkZmJ0ZwGyk3GDZSK263wv-CwAA__-ANHVW) from NEFE found that 83% of U.S. adults believe the state they live in should require a semester or yearlong course focused on personal finance as a graduation requirement, while 82% of respondents who attended high school said they wish they were required to complete a personal finance class while they were in school.

“NEFE’s data reflect strong public support for financial education in high school,” Hensley said. “The vast majority of Americans agree their state should require a semester or yearlong course for graduation, and that personal finance is equally as important as core subjects like math, science and English. Furthermore, most Americans believe the quality of their financial life would be better had they received financial education in school.”

To produce the report card, NEFE conducted detailed reviews of high school graduation requirements, state academic standards for personal finance education and laws, regulations and guidelines related to how each state delivers personal finance education in its public high schools. A national map with information on the 50 states and the District of Columbia and a downloadable copy of the [full report card is available online.](https://us.cisionone.cision.com/c/eJwsyztuKyEUANDVQMeI_wwFhZvZhnXhXp55no8D2M7yI0dpj3Qw6iVb6TlFNQe5uHl2gd8izkYqhFSCSl7LhASKXAnegyslZ16jh0ROK-k9zOaqbAmqSO3kbEEyK3tFutcvsUPdqHWBmEJAXKzQfdz19HG-xdsYj87MhemV6fX9fk8HFZrO9o_ptR51VBj1RZ3p9YBRzwM20ehxtiEyNGR6RSrw3MYE_fHNd8IKotFG0ElUjL9w_QNmLsaGxQfeImLNd2ZlevZ6UO_i__lsB2xTPnfeRyPaP19ra8MMWSRpirCQnViyU8IlMFkFctIa_or6JwAA__-SemhM)

Generative artificial intelligence is now a part of university life. A [2024 Digital Education Council survey](https://www.digitaleducationcouncil.com/resource-library-items/digital-education-council-global-ai-student-survey-2024) of 3,839 students across 16 countries found that [86%](https://campustechnology.com/articles/2024/08/28/survey-86-of-students-already-use-ai-in-their-studies.aspx) regularly used AI in their studies. It can appear during revision sessions, research and the difficult first hour of an essay. Its popularity leaves universities with a practical problem: a chatbot can produce a tidy answer in seconds, yet the information underneath may be old, incomplete or fabricated. Knowing how to ask a question is useful. Knowing when to doubt the response matters more.

Suppose an undergraduate asks a chatbot for the current [XRP to USD](https://www.binance.com/en/price/xrp) conversion rate while researching changing online data. On Sept. 20, Binance displayed an XRP price of about $1.38 and $3.5 billion in 24-hour volume. The page showed an update time of 5:54 a.m. UTC. Those figures could be different when the project is graded, so the date belongs beside them in a submission. Employment reports and scientific databases present the same research problem: what if the data changes between the time of development and review?

### Why has AI literacy become an academic priority?

Campus discussions about AI often concentrate on plagiarism, but that covers only one part of the issue. Someone can write an assignment independently and still rely on an AI’s inaccurate summary, citation of a nonexistent paper or use of a statistic stripped of context.

Advertisement

AI literacy means recognizing those risks and deciding which tasks can reasonably be handed to a tool, and what is better suited for traditional search methods. Having AI generate alternative search terms may help when a library search has stalled. But judging whether resulting papers support an academic argument cannot be delegated to a bot so easily. Sometimes the right next step for students is an office hours conversation. If an assignment is unclear, repeated prompts may produce several versions of the same mistaken assumption.

### What can go wrong when an answer sounds convincing?

A fabricated reference rarely looks obviously fake. It may include a believable title, journal name, publication year and authors whose work sounds relevant.

A student researching sleep and academic performance could receive exactly that sort of convincingly fictitious citation. It fits the topic, so it goes into the students’ notes. Later, the student searches the library database and finds nothing. The journal exists but never published the paper. One supposed author researches an unrelated subject, while the other has no matching academic record. The mistake is easy to catch once someone checks. But without that step, the reference might remain because its formatting looks right. Fluent language can give unsupported information more credibility than it deserves, increasing the risk that students miss false AI results.

Advertisement

### How can students check AI-generated claims?

Not every suggestion needs a lengthy investigation. If an AI tool proposes changing the order of two paragraphs, the risk is limited. An AI’s report of a quotation, numerical finding or description of a study deserves closer attention. The most useful habit is opening the original material. A researcher can then confirm the author, date and relevant passage. Checking sample size and methodology matters too. A genuine paper based on 30 volunteers cannot automatically support a claim about all university students.

The American Library Association’s [Framework for Information Literacy for Higher Education](https://www.ala.org/acrl/standards/ilframework) treats a source’s authority as dependent on context and research as an ongoing inquiry. A university report, personal account and peer-reviewed study may each contribute something to a student’s research, but they do not provide equivalent evidence. In the Digital Education Council [survey](https://www.digitaleducationcouncil.com/newsroom/what-students-want-key-results-from-dec-global-ai-student-survey-2024), 58% of respondents felt they lacked sufficient AI knowledge and skills. Another 72% wanted their universities to offer more training.

### How should universities set clearer AI rules?

The boundary between what constitutes AI assistance and unacceptable substitution changes between assignments. Brainstorming may be allowed in a history seminar where generated prose is prohibited. A computer science instructor might permit AI explanations of errors but require students to write and understand their submitted code.

A vague warning near the end of a syllabus does not answer common questions. Course guidance should include examples covering outlining, proofreading, translation and source discovery. Students must also know what they need to disclose.

A recent argument that professors should [retain take-home essays despite concerns about AI](https://browndailyherald.com/article/mooney-29-professors-shouldnt-abandon-the-take-home-essay-over-concerns-about-ai-20260918) reflects a wider campus dilemma. Removing take-home work could eliminate a valuable form of sustained writing. Assignments connected closely to classroom discussions, drafts and specific readings may work better than treating all unsupervised work as suspect. Disclosure can remain brief. A note saying that a tool suggested search terms or checked grammar is more useful than stating only that “AI was used.”

### Which skills will matter as AI improves?

Future AI systems may invent fewer citations and handle context more accurately. That will make them more useful, but occasional errors may also become harder to notice. A strange answer invites suspicion. A polished one often does not.

The necessary checks are ordinary research habits rather than technical expertise. Open the paper, read the quoted passage and record the date beside a changing figure. AI may shorten the route to an answer, but students still need to know where that answer came from before placing it in submitted work.

![](https://dailydodge.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Personal-Finance.png)

MADISON — The Wisconsin departments of Public Instruction and Financial Institutions have awarded $296,000 in grants to expand personal financial literacy education across the state.

The Financial Literacy Innovation Grants will fund programs at 29 schools, school districts and community organizations. The funding comes from the Department of Financial Institutions through settlement dollars designated for financial literacy education.

The grants will support implementation of Wisconsin’s personal financial literacy standards and help schools meet the requirements of Wisconsin Act 60. The law requires schools to offer a half-credit personal financial literacy course beginning with the class of 2028.

Grant recipients will develop programs, classroom activities and community events designed to help students make informed financial decisions. Some programs also will include families and community members.

“Financial literacy is about much more than understanding money,” State Superintendent Jill Underly said. “It helps students develop practical skills to make informed decisions and plan for their futures.”

DFI Secretary Wendy K. Baumann said the grants will help thousands of students build financial knowledge and prepare for adulthood.

A complete list of grant recipients and more information about the program is available on the Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction’s website.

# Childs: Sharpening our literacy game

## Marian University has an A+ rated school of education and a strong track record with something called the Science of Reading, an approach to literacy instruction built around how kids learn to read.

![Joe Childs - MHS Library Z - Horizontal.jpg](https://cdn.forumcomm.com/dims4/default/0ed366d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3947x2631+98+0/resize/840x560!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fforum-communications-production-web.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fd9%2F0e%2Fda60b00549c388c6885b5fff287b%2Fjoe-childs-mhs-library-z-horizontal.jpg)

Joe Childs

ByJoe Childs / Mitchell School District superintendent

October 07, 2026 at 7:00 AM

Opinion


Often, I visit schools in the district, and just this week, while I was in one of our elementary schools, I stepped in to take the class for a few minutes. The teacher had to step out of the room to conference with a couple of her students, so in an effort to keep the conversation going, I began talking to a classroom full of kids about their own school. I explained a bit about how the school was built, why certain hallways run the way they do, little details I still remember from watching the construction go up years ago.

Somewhere in there we landed on angles, which gave me an excuse to walk them out into the hallway and point to the spot where two corridors meet at a slant. The students and I spent a few minutes discussing the purpose, and several more minutes attempting to find the exact angle on each end. They learned something new about their own school, and I got to dust off some of those old memories. And for about 15 minutes, nobody in that hallway was thinking about anything except how those two walls met. It was a good morning.

I’m sharing this story because, that same day, we had hosted several visitors in our elementary schools for an entirely different reason, and some of what caught their attention wasn't so different from that hallway moment.

Marian University, out of Indiana, has an A+ rated school of education and a strong track record with something called the Science of Reading, an approach to literacy instruction built around how kids learn to read.

Marian has done tremendous work in the area of reading instruction and works closely with educators to share their knowledge. This year and next, Marian has teamed up with Dakota Wesleyan University to bring some of that expertise here, and our district has happily participated in a way that allows the team to watch our K-5 reading instruction up close, and we're just glad to have them in the district.

Their team recently spent three days with us, sitting in on reading blocks, meeting with our literacy coaches, and talking with teachers and administrators about how we approach reading in the early grades. They came to learn and share, and what impressed them came from two different directions.

The first was the data. A few years ago, our district made some real changes to how we teach reading in the earliest grades. Today, our youngest learners are showing academic gains that stand out even to a team that looks at literacy numbers for a living, the sort of early momentum we know pays enormous dividends the further these kids move through school. They may not have come here expecting to see work already underway, but in many ways our elementary schools have already matched what they hoped to help build.

The second thing was something no spreadsheet could have shown them. They noticed the relationships. In our schools, relationships matter. When a teacher asks a student how their new pet is doing, when our visitors notice a Dakota Wesleyan professor talking to one our teachers who had been her own student teacher a decade ago, and watched as the two of them visited like old friends catching up, because that's what they were.

More than one of our guests mentioned watching an administrator wade through a completely full hallway chatting with elementary kids about their day, in way that was just a normal Tuesday around here. Which, honestly, it is.

ADVERTISEMENT

Good reading instruction takes real expertise, and it’s a tremendous opportunity when you can bring in colleagues who've spent their careers studying it. Our literacy team has already started pulling together information about our curriculum and how our reading blocks run, so there's something solid for everyone to work with as we continue the real conversations about continuous improvement. The Marian staff showed up to help the team sharpen its game, in a way that allows everybody on the roster to stay right where they are, while we get some extra eyes and another set of very good ideas in the room.

We know that there isn’t any amount of outside expertise that creates the kind of culture that makes visiting professionals stop in a hallway and take notice. That part was already here, built from years of teachers who stay late, literacy coaches who know every kid's name, and a community that treats its schools like they matter, because they do.

Marian is going to help all of us get sharper about how we teach kids to read, and I expect good things to come from it. I also believe that one aspect that stuck with them wasn't anything in a binder. It was the sense that around here, the relationships come first, and the results follow. Put that kind of culture alongside teaching strategies and curriculum that are backed by evidence, and you've got a district that isn't just happy with where it's been, you’ve got a district excited about where it’s headed.

### AI, Title Waiver, Real Estate Auction, QC, eNote Tools; Financial Literacy Study; MBS Issuance

By: Rob Chrisman

Mon, Oct 5 2026, 11:25 AM


Today brings us the [MBA of the Carolinas](https://www.mbac.org/convention) conference, where demographics, technology, and “building a team” are on the agenda. Here at the Michigan Mortgage Lender’s Association conference in Ypsilanti, tech is certainly “on the serving platter” in the sessions, but so is how originators should best use what they have to their advantage, which includes knowledge. For example, here’s something simultaneously sobering and hopeful for lenders. Per the Census Bureau, in 2024, 58 percent of men and 56 percent of women ages [18 to 34 lived with their parents](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2026/09/parental-support-to-adult-children.html). About 2.6 million U.S. parents provided $26.6 billion in financial support to 3.7 million children. (So you don’t have to break out the calculator, that’s about $7,200 per kid.) Think of all those potential home buyers! (Today’s podcast can be found [here](https://chrismancommentary.com/podcasts/). This week’s ‘casts are presented by [Floify](https://floify.com/), the mortgage industry’s leading point-of-sale platform. Dynamic Apps, which can be seen at booth 600 during MBA Annual next week, lets lenders create fully customizable loan applications for any loan type, including HELOCs, construction, agricultural lending, non-QM and more, without custom development. Today’s has an [interview](https://chrismancommentary.com/podcasts/) Mortgage Education Institute's Andrew Conner on helping loan officers and small-to-midsize mortgage companies turn required continuing education and compliance from a burdensome, reactive “check-the-box” exercise into engaging, practical training and proactive support.)

**Financial Literacy for Kids**

The [latest NextGen Homebuyer Report](https://firsthomeiq.com/built-study/) is live, and it takes a different approach to how we think about expanding the pool of homebuyers. What if the buyers that reach your office are only a slice of the available (and interested) market? The study, "How You're Built to Buy" is a continuation in a series that has surveyed over 10,000 millennials and Gen Z, sponsored by National MI and conducted by Kristin Messerli of FirstHome IQ. According to this study, over half are anxious or avoidant with their finances, and nearly 9 in 10 experience real shame around their finances. "To me, the most interesting part of this study was that it didn't matter whether they made good money or had perfect credit and savings, at least half of them are held back by feelings of overwhelm, distrust, and anxiety," says Kristin.

**Capital Markets**

U.S. Treasuries ended the week once again weaker despite an initial rally that followed a sharply disappointing September jobs report, with nonfarm payrolls rising just 29k, unemployment increasing to 4.2 percent, wage growth slowing, and back-month revisions lower. The weak labor data increased expectations for an October Fed pause, but it has not resolved what is keeping long-term rates elevated: inflation remains above target, energy costs and sovereign-debt concerns persist, and the Fed remains cautious about easing too quickly.

The takeaway is that while hiring is clearly cooling, subdued layoffs and resilient consumer spending and business investment suggest the economy has not weakened enough to drive a sustained decline in rates, leaving the mortgage market caught between softer employment data and persistent inflation and growth pressures.

Longer-term yields, with Agency MBS tagging along, returned toward their highs by Friday's close, with the 10-year reaching 5.28 percent after touching 5.34 percent (the highest level since 2002) earlier in the week. The yield curve steepened and Agency MBS posted its worst monthly excess return (the return investors earn from MBS above the return they would have earned from a comparable-duration U.S. Treasury, capturing compensation for taking mortgage-specific risks such as prepayments, credit/liquidity, and spread volatility) at -96 basis points since March 2023, pressuring specified-pool payups, lender margins, [mortgage rates](https://www.mortgagenewsdaily.com/mortgage-rates), and applications. Rising Treasury yields, a 47 percent increase in volatility, weaker institutional demand, and longer duration weighed on prices. As most of you already know, the mortgage market is increasingly driven by purchases rather than refinancing, with Agency MBS supply reaching $111 billion last month despite refinance activity falling to its lowest share in a year. Conventional purchase issuance rose 13 percent year-over-year while refinance issuance was essentially flat. Ginnie Mae refinance issuance fell 13 percent at the same time, and UMBS 30-year issuance increased to $62 billion, with production shifting toward 6.0 percent to 6.5 percent coupons as higher mortgage rates pushed borrowers further from refinancing opportunities.

Higher rates have also created a large pool of deeply “out-of-the-money” 30-year mortgages: About $2.4 trillion of conventional MBS and $746 billion of Ginnie Mae II have little incentive to refinance, producing unusually stable prepayments and more predictable cash flows. The trade-off is greater duration risk, meaning these securities may offer attractive relative value but remain vulnerable if rates continue rising or volatility stays elevated. For those wondering how Agency MBS supply is rising year-over-year, it is not the same thing as new mortgage origination volume. MBS supply measures loans that are actually pooled and securitized, and several factors can keep that number high even when overall origination activity is falling. Agency MBS supply measures loans being pooled and securitized, not the level of new mortgage originations in real time, so issuance can remain high even as origination activity falls. Refinancing has collapsed because elevated rates make it uneconomical, but purchase lending remains active and is increasingly concentrated in higher-coupon loans, while mortgages originated in prior months can continue moving through the securitization pipeline. In short, the market is producing fewer loans overall, but a larger share of those loans are still flowing into Agency MBS, keeping supply relatively elevated even as the composition shifts away from refinances and toward purchase mortgages and higher coupons.

Looking at this week’s economic calendar, the September ISM Services index, due out today, is expected to ease modestly while continuing to signal expansion. Particular attention will be paid to whether price pressures remain elevated. Other releases of note include the August Trade Balance, Minutes from the September FOMC meeting, August Consumer Credit, August Wholesale Inventories, and Preliminary University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment. Treasury auctions will be headlined by $58 billion 3-year Treasury notes, $39 billion 10-year Treasury notes, and $22 billion 30-year Treasury bonds. We begin the week with Agency [MBS prices](https://www.mortgagenewsdaily.com/mbs) little changed from Friday’s close, the 2-year yielding 4.82, and the 10-year yielding 5.29 after closing last week at 5.28 percent, up 10-basis points over the course of last week.

by: [Nick Witwer](https://www.wearegreenbay.com/author/nick-witwer/ "Posts by Nick Witwer")

GREEN BAY, Wis. (WFRV) – The Boys and Girls Club of Green Bay got visited by a special guest as Packers linebacker and team captain Zaire Franklin stopped in to spend time and read to them.

The special visit comes as Franklin launches his ‘Tackles for Literacy’ campaign, where he has pledged to donate $44, matching his jersey number, to literacy programs for every tackle he makes this season.

> Providing the kids with the supplies and resources to be their best selves, whether that’s in school, in the classroom, or after-school programs like Boys and Girls Club, is just extremely important. When I was young, I had programs that gave me opportunities that I wasn’t getting.
>
> Zaire Franklin, Packers linebacker and team captain

Franklin’s visit to the Boys and Girls Club also came with a pizza and root beer float party, with the kids in attendance even getting to ask Franklin questions and snag some quick autographs.

So far on the season, Franklin has 29 combined tackles. He’ll look to add to that total as the Packers get ready to host the division rival Chicago Bears at Lambeau Field on Sunday at noon.
